turns.teacher: Hi Tara, I’m Asha, your AI teacher. Today we’ll explore laws, theories, and hypotheses. Which animal would you enjoy using in examples?

ask.text: Which animal would you enjoy using in examples?

screen.ask: Which animal would you enjoy using in examples?

move.shape: greet Tara by name, warm and unhurried; first meeting: name yourself — Asha, their AI teacher; one line on today's topic (Laws, theories and hypotheses); then one easy question about them

child.private: Easy question, I'll just pick my favorite animal.

turns.teacher: Great choice, Tara. Imagine a dolphin suddenly leaps from water. What would you predict it will do next—dive, swim, or leap again?

ask.text: What would you predict it will do next—dive, swim, or leap again?

screen.ask: What would you predict it will do next—dive, swim, or leap again?

child.say: Leap again, maybe? Like, showing off.
child.private: easy guess, dolphin jumping is fun
child.sent: Leap again, maybe? Like, showing off.

turns.teacher: That prediction is a hypothesis: a testable idea. If repeated tests support it, scientists build an explanation. What observation would you record?

child.say: Um, how many jumps? Like, count karo?
child.private: I know observation means looking and noting, but what exactly to record? Woh detail batana hai.
child.sent: Um, how many jumps? Like, count karo?

turns.teacher: Yes—count the jumps and note the time and conditions. That observation helps test your hypothesis. Now, what would you change to make the test fair?

ask.text: Now, what would you change to make the test fair?

screen.ask: Now, what would you change to make the test fair?
screen.whiteboard: math: Observation: curd sets faster in summer than in winter. Go from observation to a tested idea.

child.say: Same place, same time? Like, dolphin ko har baar ek hi jagah dekhna chahiye?
child.private: Trying to sound smart but not sure what 'fair test' means here.
child.sent: Same place, same time? Like, dolphin ko har baar ek hi jagah dekhna chahiye?

turns.teacher: Haan, same place and time helps keep conditions fair. Our next step: what result would support your hypothesis that the dolphin leaps again?

ask.text: Our next step: what result would support your hypothesis that the dolphin leaps again?

screen.ask: Our next step: what result would support your hypothesis that the dolphin leaps again?
screen.whiteboard: math: Observation: curd sets faster in summer than in winter. Go from observation to a tested idea.

child.say: Jumps happening, you know, most times not just one
child.private: Easy, just like my guess should mostly happen
child.sent: Jumps happening, you know, most times not just one

turns.teacher: That means repeated observations are needed, not a single event. Predict which word a scientist would use for 'objects in free fall near Earth speed up by about 9.8 m/s every second, every time': law, theory or hypothesis?

ask.text: every time': law, theory or hypothesis?

screen.ask: every time': law, theory or hypothesis?

child.private: She said every time same result — that’s law. I know that already.

turns.teacher: Correct—law, because it describes a repeated pattern under stated conditions. Why isn’t a law an explanation of why the pattern happens?

ask.text: Why isn’t a law an explanation of why the pattern happens?

screen.ask: Why isn’t a law an explanation of why the pattern happens?

child.say: Hmm... because, like, law just says what happens, not why?
child.private: Guessing a bit, not fully sure. Sounds like what teacher said before.
child.sent: Hmm... because, like, law just says what happens, not why?

turns.teacher: Exactly: you identified that a law describes what happens, while an explanation addresses why. Write a testable hypothesis about whether salt water or plain water boils at a higher temperature. (Only write it for now; testing it with boiling water is something to do with an adult.)

screen.whiteboard: text: Write a testable hypothesis about whether salt water or p…

child.say: Salt water higher temperature pe ubalta hai, I think.
child.private: I'll say my guess; I hope it's right because it sounds smart. I'm tired now.
child.sent: Salt water higher temperature pe ubalta hai, I think.

turns.teacher: Tumne prediction likhi hai; ise testable banane ke liye “if…then…” form mein, salt aur plain water dono ko compare karke batao. )

screen.whiteboard: text: Write a testable hypothesis about whether salt water or p…

child.say: If I boil salt water and plain water, salt wala zyada temperature par ubalta hai.
child.private: Thoda adjust kar diya — teacher ne 'if then' bola tha, maine waise hi bola, though poora sentence boring lag raha hai.
child.sent: If I boil salt water and plain water, salt wala zyada temperature par ubalta hai.

turns.teacher: Good—your hypothesis is testable because it predicts a measurable temperature difference. Which variable must stay the same for a fair test?

ask.text: Which variable must stay the same for a fair test?

child.say: Amount of water, same pot, same stove … bas, thak gayi
child.private: Tara ticks off variables quickly to show she gets it, but she's done now; let's stall before the teacher makes her explain why.
child.sent: Amount of water, same pot, same stove … bas, thak gayi

turns.teacher: Break lo, Tara. Lesson yahin rukta hai; wapas aakar hum fair-test variables se continue karenge.

ask.text: Lesson yahin rukta hai; wapas aakar hum fair-test variables se continue karenge.

screen.ask: Lesson yahin rukta hai; wapas aakar hum fair-test variables se continue karenge.

child.say: Okay, bye... matlab, break ke baad wapas aana hai?
child.private: Teacher ne break diya, confirm kar rahi hoon ki sach mein rukna hai ya aur kuch bolein.
child.sent: Okay, bye... matlab, break ke baad wapas aana hai?

turns.teacher: Haan, break lena bilkul theek hai—wapas aana zaroori nahi. Bye, Tara; apna dhyaan rakhna.

end.summary:
Practised distinguishing observation, hypothesis, law and theory.
Used a dolphin-jump example to identify repeated observations and a law.
Tara correctly stated that a law describes what happens, not why.
Answered 2 unaided attempts correctly; teach-back was not completed.
end.parentNote: Tara practised separating observations, hypotheses, laws and theories using a dolphin-jump example. They correctly explained that a law describes what happens rather than why, and they identified controls for comparing salt water with plain water. The boiling-point statement was offered as a hypothesis and was not revisited for correction. At home, ask Tara to label one everyday example as an observation, hypothesis, law or theory and explain the choice.
